## Sampling and acoustic activity

After accounting for nights without usable acoustic recordings, the environmental-model dataset contained 1,056 site-nights from eight sites. Sampling extended from late April through mid-October 2015. Sampling effort was uneven among sites because of detector failures and other periods without usable acoustic data, with the number of retained nights ranging from 47 at BUL18 to 174 at several sites.

Across these 1,056 site-nights, aggregate bat activity totaled 103,681 5-min detection intervals. The species-level dataset contained 17 species, and the frequency-group datasets were constructed for the same 1,056 site-nights, with 7,078, 27,602, and 69,001 detection intervals assigned to the low-, mid-, and high-frequency groups, respectively.

## Model development and adequacy

Model development materially improved representation of the observed ecological and sampling structure. Initial Poisson models showed strong residual temporal dependence, with lag-1 residual correlation of approximately 0.80 and correlations remaining above 0.50 through a 14-day lag. Replacing the Poisson likelihood with a negative-binomial likelihood accounted for substantial extra-Poisson variation but did not eliminate the temporal structure.

Allowing seasonal phenology to vary among sites using a penalized factor-smooth interaction produced a much larger improvement. In the final aggregate conditional model, lag-1 residual correlation was 0.379, declined to 0.208 at lag 2 and 0.168 at lag 3, was near zero by lag 4, and became weakly negative at longer lags. This pattern indicated that much of the apparent serial dependence in simpler models reflected unmodeled differences in seasonal phenology among sites rather than a persistent autoregressive observation process.

The final aggregate conditional model also showed satisfactory MCMC behavior. All reported $\hat{R}$ values were 1.00, with large bulk and tail effective sample sizes. Seven of 12,000 post-warmup transitions reached the maximum tree depth of 12. Posterior predictive checks reproduced the broad response distribution and site-specific means well. Site-specific predictive variation was less exact: the model tended to overpredict variability at BUC3, BUL11, and LBL5 and modestly underpredict it at some other sites. We therefore retained the biologically interpretable site-specific seasonal structure rather than increasing model complexity solely to reproduce all remaining distributional features.

## Seasonal activity

Seasonal activity varied nonlinearly across the sampling period, and the inferred seasonal pattern changed substantially after accounting for nightly environmental conditions (@fig-seasonality). In the total seasonal model, equal-site averaged activity declined through May, increased to a first summer maximum in June, declined in July, and increased again in early August before falling through September and October (@fig-seasonality`a`). After conditioning on nightly temperature, relative humidity, and lunar phase, the seasonal trajectory was markedly different: activity was highest early in the sampling season, declined sharply from May into June, and remained comparatively low through most of the summer and autumn, with only modest increases in August and September (@fig-seasonality`b`). Thus, much of the pronounced mid-summer structure in the total seasonal pattern was associated with seasonal variation in the measured environmental conditions, while the conditional day-of-year effect was dominated by elevated activity early in the sampling season. Seasonal phenology also differed substantially among sites in both the magnitude and timing of activity (@fig-seasonality`c`), supporting the use of site-specific seasonal smooths rather than a single common seasonal trajectory.

## Echolocation-frequency groups

Characteristic-frequency groups contributed very different amounts of total recorded activity. High-frequency species accounted for 69,001 detection intervals, compared with 27,602 for the mid-frequency group and 7,078 for the low-frequency group. Consequently, the aggregate community response was numerically dominated by high-frequency detections, although the frequency-stratified models allow the environmental responses of the three groups to be evaluated separately.

### Temperature responses among frequency groups

Temperature was positively associated with bat activity across all three frequency groups over the well-sampled portion of the observed temperature gradient, although response shape differed among groups (@fig-temperature). Across the central 80% of observed nightly temperatures (6.07–17.3 $^\circ$C), predicted activity increased from 1.52 to 13.7 intervals night$^{-1}$ for the low-frequency group, from 3.48 to 69.9 intervals night$^{-1}$ for the mid-frequency group, and from 33.9 to 68.3 intervals night${^-1}$ for the high-frequency group. The corresponding median increases were 12.2 (89% CrI: 9.50–15.5), 66.4 (54.4–81.0), and 34.3 (26.7–42.4) intervals night$^{-1}$, respectively, with posterior probability of an increase equal to 1.00 for each group. Low- and mid-frequency activity continued to increase toward the warm end of the observed gradient, whereas high-frequency activity increased through most of the well-sampled temperature range before leveling off and declining at warmer temperatures. Across posterior draws, the median temperature associated with maximum high-frequency activity was 18.8 $^\circ$C (89% CrI: 17.3–24.2 $^\circ$C); 16.9% of posterior curves placed the maximum at the upper boundary of the observed temperature range, indicating greater uncertainty in the shape of the response at the warmest temperatures.

### Frequency-dependent humidity responses

Relative humidity was associated with markedly different patterns of activity among frequency groups (@fig-humidity). Across the central 80% of observed nightly relative humidity conditions (49.4–84.6%), expected activity declined substantially for both the mid- and high-frequency groups. For high-frequency bats, expected activity decreased from 52.4 to 29.0 5-min detection intervals night$^{-1}$, corresponding to a median ratio of 0.55 (89% CrI: 0.50–0.62) and a posterior probability of a decrease of 1.00. Mid-frequency activity declined from 19.8 to 13.7 intervals night$^{-1}$ over the same humidity range (median ratio = 0.69, 89% CrI: 0.58–0.83; posterior probability of decrease > 0.999). In contrast, low-frequency activity showed little evidence of an overall decline, increasing slightly from 4.32 to 5.32 intervals night$^{-1}$ (median ratio = 1.23, 89% CrI: 0.97–1.56; posterior probability of decrease = 0.083). Response curves were nonlinear, particularly for the mid-frequency group, but declines became pronounced at high relative humidity for both the mid- and high-frequency groups, whereas activity of the low-frequency group remained comparatively insensitive across the observed humidity gradient.

### Lunar responses among frequency groups

Associations between lunar illumination and bat activity also differed among frequency groups (@fig-lunar). High-frequency activity increased with lunar illumination, with expected activity increasing by 10.4 5-min detection intervals per night from new moon to full moon (89% CrI: 7.02–14.4). This corresponded to a 1.28-fold increase in expected activity (89% CrI: 1.18–1.39), with essentially all posterior draws supporting an increase. Low-frequency activity showed weaker evidence of a response in the opposite direction, declining by a median of 0.92 intervals per night from new moon to full moon (89% CrI: −2.06–0.25; posterior probability of a decrease = 0.898). Mid-frequency activity exhibited a nonlinear relationship with lunar illumination, but the overall new- to full-moon contrast was comparatively small and uncertain (median difference = 1.81 intervals per night, 89% CrI: −1.00–4.80; posterior probability of an increase = 0.850). Thus, the clearest lunar response occurred among high-frequency bats, for which activity increased across the lunar illumination gradient.
